div.p: The museum acquisition of natively digital works raises specific issues related to their materiality, but also to the appropriation of technology by artists. Digital materiality is characterized by the encoding of information in the form of bits and its restitution through the execution of computer scripts, opening the door to automated programming of artistic objects. Works within the realm of digital art (profiled since the 1960s with computational art), and later net art (starting in the 1990s), rely on computer protocols: these protocols establish standards for processing information within complex technological systemsGalloway, 2004. The advent of blockchain technology in 2008 and its developments towards the creation of the NFT format paved the way for new protocols in the creation and exchange of art.

NFTs (Non-Fungible Tokens) are certification files listed on a blockchain: a shared digital ledger compiles information within successive blocks that are linked and protected by cryptographic protocols. An NFT is defined as a document set that includes three components: content, a certificate of ownership, and a smart contract. 1) The content of an NFT can be an artistic object (a work or part of a work) or a reproduction of a work of art. It is most often presented as a digital file of still or animated images, videos, or music. These files are usually stored on an external storage system (off-chain), but in the case of generative works, the computer code that generates the work can also be stored on the blockchain (on-chain). 2) The certificate attests to the properties of the content, such as its unique identifier and the address of the owner's digital wallet. Non-reproducible and presented as unfalsifiable, it establishes ownership and keeps track of successive owners. The certificate is not a guarantee of authenticity (in the sense of a legitimate origin of the work, as many fakes exist in the NFT market), but rather a mechanism for identifying provenance and traceability that records the circulation of the work within the technical network. 3) The smart contract sets the terms of transfer and sale of the NFT (payment terms, transfer of ownership, resale rights for the artist). The terms of this contract self-execute at the time of the transaction.

As a new protocol for recording assets, the NFT system opens up possibilities for documenting, managing reproducibility, and marketing works. It is used to create scarcity: in the context of the infinite reproducibility of digital files, certifying unique pieces and limited editions is a major challengeRinehart, 2006, which the blockchain claims to address. The smart contract is also a way to codify the transfer of ownership of works. In this regard, the NFT format resonates with concerns raised as early as the 1970s by figures in conceptual art regarding the economic circuits of art. For instance, art dealer and curator Seth Siegelaub proposed codifying the legal terms of art acquisition in the document The Artist’s Reserved Rights Transfer and Sale Agreement (1971); in collaboration with lawyer Robert Projansky). The specificity of the NFT format here is to make transfer contracts programmable and automatable.

Blockchain technology protocols have also become a medium for experimentation in artistic practices since 2014Catlow et al., 2017. Part of the NFT artistic production can thus be categorized as protocol-based works. Two main types can be identified. The first is the contractual protocol work: the piece Smart Burn Contract #11 – Hoarder (2022) by artist Jonas Lund is an example. Acquired by the Centre Pompidou in 2023, it stipulates that the owner of this NFT cannot sell any work from their collection, thereby creating a contractual obligation between the artist and the museum. The instructions for the work specify that if the contract terms are violated, the NFT will be destroyed (burned) by the artist and disappear from the museum's digital wallet. NFT protocol works update a practice already evident in conceptual art, which can be seen with Yves Klein's Chéquier (1959), a work created as transaction receipts. Jonas Lund's piece echoes this approach by exploiting the technological functions of controlling the circulation of works offered by blockchain.

A second type of practice is the creation of generative protocol works: the artist programs a creation system based on algorithms that automatically generate works through the random combination of preselected elements. This approach is in line with the experiments of minimalist and conceptual artists who devised mathematical systems to generate composition grids (such as Sol LeWitt's Wall Drawings), a practice later taken up and developed in digital artMcCormack et al., 2014. In the case of NFT works, the script can be encoded directly onto the blockchain, and the works generated by the code's execution are automatically recorded there. Canadian artist Dmitri Cherniak thus created a series of works called Ringers (2021): 1000 NFTs based on a common geometric vocabulary. They were generated by activating a script at the moment of each edition's online acquisition. The Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) acquired one of these editions in 2023 (Ringers #962).

As the museumification of NFTs is very recent, there are still few specific acquisition protocols for this format to govern their integration into museum collections. While the ZKM (Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe) pioneered in acquiring a handful of NFTs as early as 2018, it wasn't until 2021 that a significant series of museum acquisitions took place (Whitney Museum, MAK Museum of Applied Arts Vienna, Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), Institute of Contemporary Art Miami, San José Museum of Art, Francisco Carolinum, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMoMA), Musée Granet, Centre Pompidou). The shift from the Ethereum blockchain to a more energy-efficient system in 2022 eliminated an irritant for the museum world. Like other types of natively digital works, the integration of NFTs into museum collections calls for the implementation of protocols to prevent technological obsolescenceLacerte, 2007. NFTs also present a specific challenge in terms of administrative protocol: purchasing works with cryptocurrency, managing access to the digital wallet where they are stored, and the movement of works between wallets create a new challenge for museums. The ZKM experienced this firsthand: a migration error between wallet addresses led to the loss of access to two CryptoPunks (LarvaLabs), iconic pieces of crypto art that are now out of reachBatycka, 2022.
